data.title: Watch live: Trump takes campaign blitz to Georgia
data.description:
President Trump heads to Georgia Friday afternoon as Republicans look to gain ground in a closely watched Senate race with less than three weeks until the midterms.

Trump is expected to rally support for Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who is challenging incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff (D). The president will also appear alongside Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson, who is facing former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D).

The visit comes after Collins and Ossoff clashed in a heated debate Tuesday over Trump’s policies, the economy and the Iran war. The Democrat has maintained a narrow lead in recent polls, adding pressure on the GOP as early voting is already underway in the Peach State.

The event in Dalton, Ga., is scheduled to begin at 2:45 p.m. EDT.

Watch live above.

data.title: Live updates: Zacharia exits White House post; Trump heads to Georgia campaign stop
data.description:
Katie Zacharia is on her way to being a former White House press secretary, after President Trump told reporters he told her to “reconsider” the position and amid a rocky start to the job this week, a White House official told The Hill.

Zacharia faced scrutiny over her legal credentials and held a short press briefing since starting the job on Monday.

Trump travels Friday to Georgia, for another stop on his red state campaigning sweep.

After visits to Alabama, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Texas, Tennessee and Kentucky over the past few weeks, he plans to make his way back to the South, where he’s slated to speak to voters Friday afternoon in Dalton, Ga.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) is joining Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for the second day of a multicity campaigning effort throughout Michigan as he gears up to face off against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) on Election Day.

The New York lawmaker was an early supporter of El-Sayed this election season, also campaigning for him ahead of Michigan’s Democratic primary this summer.

Follow live below.

data.title: Washington Post says photographer attacked by Israeli settlers
data.description:
The Washington Post’s executive editor said Friday that Israeli settlers attacked one of its photojournalists, who was working on assignment in the West Bank.

“She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.” Matt Murray wrote in a statement shared to social platform X. “We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job.”

A video capturing the incident — shared by The Post — appeared to show masked Israeli settlers attacking photographer Heidi Levine while she was on the ground, kicking her in the stomach. Separate posts by independent journalist Andrey Khrzhanovskiy, a pro-Palestinian activist, alleged the assailants also beat her with sticks.

“They took everything. They took all my stuff,” Levine said in the video when Khrzhanovskiy and other nearby journalists came to her aid. “They just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times.”

After a few moments, the masked settlers began chasing Levine and the group that helped her.

Levine’s alleged assault was a part of masked settlers’ attack on a West Bank village’s annual harvest, where the attackers reportedly burned olive trees and threw rocks at Palestinians, according to Reuters — citing witnesses to the incident. The bystanders told the publication that 80 masked people carrying gas canisters had descended upon the gathering.

Palestinian medics treated Levine at a hospital in Ramallah, a city north of Jerusalem, Murray said. He added that she is now “safe.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the attack in a Friday morning statement, saying, “Israel unequivocally condemns violence against anyone—Jews, Arabs, Christians or journalists. Those responsible will be held accountable.”

But Netanyahu also called into question who started the encounter, as “reports indicate some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths,” he said.

The Israel prime minister added that “masked individuals on both sides [were] hurling objects,” and other recordings appear “to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual.”

“The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence,” he concluded. 

The Israeli Defense Force (IDF) and Israel Border Police similarly decried the incident and confirmed its forces had responded to it, saying, “All details of the incident will be examined. Upon arriving to the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means.”

“At another location where the confrontation took place, IDF soldiers initially fired warning shots into the air and then fired toward a suspect who ran toward them, carrying a sharp object and posed a threat to them. The confrontation was dispersed,” the IDF stated.

data.title: New dinosaur species identified from fossil tucked away in a museum
data.description:
(NewsNation) — A fossil stored in a London museum for more than a century has been identified as a new species of dinosaur.

Researchers say the new dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina, was identified from a skull fragment at the Natural History Museum. The fossil was first found by Reginald Walter Tooley, an amateur paleontologist, at the base of a cliff on the Isle of Wight.

After Tooley died, the museum acquired the fossil in 1924, along with more than 1,000 other specimens he had collected.

“It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years,” said the study’s lead author, Dr. Cassius Morrison, in a press release.

Researchers used CT scans to make 3D images of the skull and the area where the dinosaur’s brain would have been. When they compared these images to other meat-eating dinosaurs, they found some unusual features. These included an oval-shaped opening where the spinal cord met the brain and a ridge shaped like an hourglass. These differences led them to decide it was a new species.

Invictibellatrix was part of a group of meat-eating dinosaurs called megaraptorans, which were related to tyrannosaurs. It had a long, narrow head, small arms, and probably had feathers. Its claws were between 4 and 8 inches long. The dinosaur was about 10 to 13 feet long and stood around 5 feet tall, making it one of the smallest and earliest megaraptorans found so far.

Scientists believe it lived in what is now the United Kingdom about 120 million years ago. Its name means ‘unconquered female warrior,’ a reference to the group’s later role as top predators.

“It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex,” Morrison said.

“We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight,” he continued. “They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small.”

The researchers published their findings in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

data.title: El-Sayed mocks Vance's 'cute little' Michigan rally
data.description:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed mocked Vice President Vance’s  recent visit to Michigan, calling it “a cute little rally.”

“JD Vance was just in Michigan. He had a cute little rally in Monroe,” El-Sayed said during an event. “He invited the like, I don’t know, five people who like him.”

Vance visited Monroe, Mich., to rally support for former Rep. Mike Rogers (R), who is facing El-Sayed in a competitive Senate race to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D).

During the campaign rally, Vance attacked El-Sayed and said Michigan deserves a better candidate, a video clip posted by the New York Post shows.

“You deserve better than a little weasel who should shut his mouth and show a little gratitude to the country that gave him everything,” Vance said addressing the crowd. “You deserve a senator who is grateful to this country.”

The Michigan Democrat responded to Vance’s “little weasel” remark by saying, “What you’re talking about is a f—— wolverine.”

In his speech, El-Sayed mentioned that Vance wanted to raise questions about his commitment to America and said he “got a front row seat to what my life might have been had I not been born in America. So don’t lecture me about America I know America.”

“Let me tell you nobody understands how deep and profound the gift of this country is like a kid who was born here but for the accident of history that allowed that to happen,” the Democratic candidate continued.

The rally comes a little over two weeks ahead of the November midterm elections, as Republicans fight to maintain congressional majority.

While Vance rallied to show support for Rogers, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) is joining El-Sayed for the second day of a multicity campaigning effort throughout Michigan.

data.title: Trump says he told Zacharia to 'reconsider' press secretary role
data.description:
President Trump told reporters on Friday that he told Katie Zacharia that she should” reconsider” her role as White House press secretary after her rocky start to the job this week. 

“I said, ‘honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,'” Trump told reporters, referring to a conversation he said he had with Zacharia earlier. 

“I said, ‘you think about it, but I would reconsider,'” he continued. 

Trump told reporters the decision is ultimately up to Zacharia, but that the decision was up to her. When asked how much time he will give her, Trump said he will talk to her when he gets back. The president is heading to Georgia for a rally then to Florida for much of the weekend.

Trump said he wants Zacharia “to be happy” and said the news media has treated unfairly.

data.title: Can voters learn to stop worrying and love Big AI?
data.description:
Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), who told me he uses chatbots “all the time,” appears confident Republicans are misplaying their hand with the AI industry. Americans have reason to feel that the AI revolution is “something that is happening to them, not for them,” Schiff told me. “AI industry leaders themselves have been clear about the need for federal safeguards. Unenforceable voluntary commitments and self-regulation will not cut it.”

A few Tuesdays earlier, the mood at the White House had been considerably more celebratory. President Trump hosted a who’s who of tech titans in Washington, D.C., for the signing of an AI safety pact. (Sorry, superintelligence or “SI.”) The meeting yielded what Trump called a “morally binding” agreement to develop AI for the common good. The means of securing this happy outcome is to entrust the industry to “self-police” and “self-regulate” rather than face federal regulation.

Will Americans accept an industry’s freedom to remake their lives as the price of national greatness? Trump has made that bet on his party’s behalf — a stark contrast, at least in rhetoric, to what he said back in June. Asked about Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-Vt.) proposal for public ownership of AI, he said, “There’s something very interesting about it, where it almost becomes a partnership with the American public,” according to the Associated Press. Trump also told reporters that his voters and Sanders’s “aren’t that far apart” on economics. If that much is true, then — as some Republican candidates are now discovering — the promise of American supremacy should offer limited comfort to Americans who suspect they’ll have little say in the terms of their own future.

Advocates of AI deregulation have found a receptive audience in Washington, with Republican candidates adopting their refrain: let Big AI move fast and break things, lest China get there first. “Under [the] Bernie Sanders plan, a two-year moratorium, that is dangerous to the national security of our country because in two years, China is going to be so far ahead, we’re going to be in so much trouble,” said Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) in a Senate debate days ago after her Democratic opponent dubbed her “Data Center Darline.”

While Democrats are clearly fractured over AI — with many, including Schiff, opposed to such lengthy moratoriums — some Republicans facing tough elections seem to doubt the marching orders from Trump’s White House will help them win. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for governor in Wisconsin who in January called data centers an “exciting new technology” and voted in Congress to speed up their permitting, released a James Fishback-style “aura farming” edit video immediately following the primary election distinguishing himself from his opponent “Data Center David Crowley.” In Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers backed a yearlong moratorium on data center construction two weeks after affordability champion Abdul El-Sayed became the Democratic nominee, while continuing to attack El-Sayed’s support for public ownership of AI.

There is a clear mismatch between voters’ misgivings on the ground and the way Trump wants to get around the problem: that if he can get Americans excited enough about “Super Intelligence,” his party’s political liabilities will take care of themselves. “These Republicans who are responding to public sentiment and doing something about AI are the ones in competitive races. They’re not getting orders from the top,” Saikat Chakrabarti, the progressive tech multimillionaire and former Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) chief of staff, told me.

Democrats’ quarrels may yet prove an advantage: a party still arguing about AI gives its candidates, especially progressives who decline Big AI’s super PAC money, latitude to articulate the public’s misgivings. “The Schiff wing is saying we should do some regulation because I know we have to say we have to do some regulation,” Chakrabarti continued. “I think the Bernie wing is taking it the most seriously, but even that answer right now is let’s pause and figure it out. Whoever has the answer to that next crisis is going to win 90 percent of the country in the next election.”

Schiff, for his part, told me he is working on a legislative proposal “[rethinking] what unemployment compensation will look like” and other things, to be introduced in the coming months. There is, at least, some figuring out underway.

Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, whom the Democratic campaign of James Talarico has shelled with ads about his ambiguous support for data centers, sounds less than delighted. “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign,” he lamented in private, “like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming — you know — from DC. I don’t control the message or what we’re doing.”

Paxton, like Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, now backs tighter restrictions on data center development after previously taking a more supportive stance. Republicans are making a considerable wager that the prospect of winning the AI arms race will reconcile Americans to whatever the industry has planned for them. They’re increasingly finding themselves drawn into the same arguments now consuming Democrats, whatever the president would prefer.

William Liang is a writer living in San Francisco. He volunteers for Connie Chan’s congressional campaign in California’s 11th District.

data.title: Musk settles election lottery lawsuits over $1 million voter giveaways
data.description:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk agreed to settle two lawsuits over his $1 million check handouts to battleground voters in the 2024 election, according to court filings published Thursday.

The suits, filed in the Western District of Texas, accused the Tesla and SpaceX CEO of defrauding voters when his political action committee (PAC), America PAC, offered a $1 million giveaway to swing state voters every day leading up to the 2024 general election.

Musk first made the pledge in October 2024 in Pennsylvania, and eventually made similar promises in Michigan, Nevada, Arizona, Georgia, Wisconsin and North Carolina.

“The only thing we ask for the million dollars is that you be a spokesperson for the petition,” Musk told a recipient he handpicked from the audience at the time.

The lawsuits argued that voters were misled when they signed the petition and were told recipients would be chosen at “random” as in a lottery. Musk told a Philadelphia judge that winners were not chosen by random but chosen to be paid “spokespeople for the group.”

The tech mogul was ordered to testify under oath in June but had not yet testified before the settlements were reached. The details of the settlement were not included in public filings, and The Hill reached out to the plaintiffs’ and Musk’s legal teams for more information.

In Wisconsin, Musk made a different pledge for $1 million check handouts to voters during the state’s Supreme Court election last year.

Musk initially announced in March 2025 that he would speak in Wisconsin, with entrance limited to those who had voted in the state’s Supreme Court election. He said on the social platform X he would “personally hand over two checks for a million dollars each in appreciation for you taking the time to vote.”

About 12 hours later, his post was deleted and replaced with another, clarifying entrance was limited to those who signed the petition against “activist judges.” Musk said the money would be given to “spokesmen” for the petition, and he went to hand out two checks during a campaign rally in Wisconsin.

La Crosse County, Wisc. District Attorney Tim Gruenke (D) announced in August his office declined to press charges over the handouts, arguing that in the end, “nobody was paid anything of value for voting or promising to vote.”

Despite Musk’s efforts, the conservative candidate he backed, Brad Schimel, lost to Democratic-backed Susan Crawford, keeping the high court’s liberal majority.

While Musk has not made similar pledges this election cycle, the SpaceX CEO is shaping up to be the largest known donor of the 2026 midterms for Republicans.

data.title: Brown, Acton both up 6 points in Ohio races: poll
data.description:
A new poll of the Ohio Senate and gubernatorial races shows Democrats ahead in both contests.

In the Senate race, a Bowling Green State University (BGSU) poll found former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) ahead of Sen. Jon Husted (R) by six points, 48 percent to 42 percent, among likely voters. When BGSU surveyed the race in September, Brown had just a three-point lead.

Ohio voters are evenly split 48 to 48 on who they think will win, regardless of who they support. That is narrower from September, when more thought Husted would win.

In the governor’s race, Democrat Amy Acton leads Republican Vivek Ramaswamy also by six points, 50 percent to 44 percent. In BGSU’s September poll, Acton had a three-point lead. Most still think Ramaswamy is likely to win in the end, 55 to 43, though that is a closer margin than in BGSU’s September poll.

Ohio was long a battleground state but has moved towards Republicans in the last decade, starting with President Trump’s win in 2016. Former Vice President Harris lost Ohio by 11 points in 2024, and Brown lost his Senate seat that year by 3.5 points.

BGSU notes in its survey that Democrats in Ohio are more motivated to vote than Republicans, 59 percent to 41 percent, a narrower edge than in BGSU’s September poll.

BGSU Political Science Professor Robert Alexander said while Democrats may be ahead now, they should not celebrate just yet.

“While this will be welcome news to Democrats, a blue wave in Ohio is far from a sure thing,” Alexander said. “Republicans have closed well in recent statewide elections, and I would be surprised if these races did not end up within the margin of error in either direction.”

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, agrees that the Ohio race is close, giving Brown just a 53 percent shot at flipping the seat.

The battleground Senate races have been inundated with political ads throughout the cycle, and Ohio voters expressed fatigue in the BGSU poll.

Just 6 percent of likely Ohio voters want to see more political ads before Election Day, while 60 percent say the ads are largely negative, which has caused them to tune out campaign ads altogether.

“Ohio voters remain deeply engaged in this election, but they are also telling us that the nonstop barrage of political advertising has become overwhelming,” Alexander said. 

The BGSU poll, conducted in partnership with YouGov, was a web-based survey of 1,000 likely Ohio voters fielded from Sept. 29-Oct. 9. The margin of error is +/- 3.95 points.

data.title: AI safety group pushes for tighter export controls, limits on 'vastly superhuman AI'
data.description:
A conservative AI safety group is calling for the U.S. to implement tighter restrictions on advanced chip sales to China and limit the development of “vastly superhuman AI” as part of a new framework for AI policy.

Humans First, chaired by former Tea Party leader Amy Kremer, laid out what it described as an “America First” policy framework.

“AI will supercharge our nation’s economy, improve our quality of life, and ensure we dominate around the world,” it wrote. “But policy must always be focused on helping hardworking Americans and putting Humans First.”

The group is arguing for stricter export controls on high-end chips and other AI technologies, mandatory testing of models for extreme risks, mandatory public reporting of major AI incidents, developer liability for “reckless design” and a “red line” on self-improving AI.

It also called for an end to any federal use of Flock cameras and warrantless searches of private data, in addition to urging a halt in H-1B visa approvals and opposing federal preemption of state AI laws.

Humans First, which was initially created to organize across party lines, shifted its focus to conservative activists in April when it tapped Kremer to serve as chair.

The group has been a vocal critic of the data center buildout in recent months, leading a day of nationwide demonstrations in July and staging a cross-country bus tour opposing the AI infrastructure that wrapped up earlier this month.

The group’s AI framework stands in contrast to the more hands-off approach currently championed by President Trump, who has argued stricter regulations could hamper the U.S.’s ability to compete with China.

Trump gathered major AI leaders at the White House late last month, where they signed onto a series of voluntary commitments to place internal controls on their models and allow for external auditing.
